modes.label: νₛ(OCO)
modes.note: Both C=O bonds stretch in phase while C stays put — the totally symmetric stretch, conventionally ν₁. Centrosymmetric, so by the mutual exclusion rule it's IR-inactive but Raman-active.

modes.label: δ(OCO)
modes.note: Both O's swing the same way in-plane while C recoils oppositely, closing and opening the O-C-O angle — the in-plane component of the doubly-degenerate bend, conventionally ν₂. Degenerate with the out-of-plane wagging component below; together the pair is why ν₂ is IR-active.

modes.label: ω(OCO)
modes.note: The same ν₂ bending motion as above, but out of the molecular plane — shown here as the atoms pulsing in size rather than a real 2D displacement, since a flat diagram can't otherwise depict out-of-plane motion. Frequency-coincident with the in-plane scissoring component, so it has no separately resolved band of its own.

modes.label: νₐₛ(OCO)
modes.note: One C=O bond lengthens as the other shortens, in antiphase — the asymmetric stretch, conventionally ν₃. Breaks the molecule's center of symmetry, making it IR-active (and, by the mutual exclusion rule, Raman-inactive).

modes.label: νₛ(CH₄)
modes.note: All four C-H bonds stretch in phase, lengthening and shortening together — the totally symmetric stretch of this tetrahedral molecule. Doesn't change the molecule's dipole moment at all (it stays exactly zero throughout, by symmetry), so it's IR-forbidden — observed only in Raman. A₁.

modes.label: δ(HCH)
modes.note: Two H-C-H angles open while the other two close, in a complementary pattern — the doubly-degenerate bending mode. Shown here as one representative component of the pair (a second, independent component exists at the same frequency, related to this one by the molecule's own symmetry operations — not separately drawn). Like ν₁, doesn't change the dipole moment, so it's IR-forbidden — Raman-active only. E (doubly degenerate).

modes.label: νₐₛ(CH₄)
modes.note: One C-H bond stretches while the others adjust to compensate — the triply-degenerate asymmetric stretch. Shown here as one representative component of three (the other two, related by the molecule's own symmetry operations, sit at the same frequency and aren't separately drawn). This genuinely changes the dipole moment, making it IR-active — the dominant C-H stretching band in methane's infrared spectrum. T₂ (triply degenerate).

modes.label: δ(HCH)
modes.note: The H atoms rock back and forth relative to the central carbon — the triply-degenerate bending mode. Shown here as one representative component of three, same caveat as ν₃ above. Also IR-active, since it changes the dipole moment too — together with ν₃, these are the two modes responsible for methane's strong infrared absorption (and its potency as a greenhouse gas, since both fall in the thermal-infrared window Earth radiates through). T₂ (triply degenerate).

modes.label: ν(CO)
modes.note: C and O move apart and together along the single bond — the only vibration a two-atom molecule can have, so there's no symmetric/asymmetric pair and nothing to number ν₁/ν₂/ν₃-style.

modes.label: ν(CO)
modes.note: C and O still just move apart and together along the bond, same motion as free-gas ν(CO) above — bonded end-on (atop) to a single metal atom, retaining the molecule's own C∞v symmetry. Metal→CO π-backdonation into the antibonding 2π* orbital weakens and lengthens the C-O bond relative to the gas phase, red-shifting this stretch well below the free CO value (2143 cm⁻¹) even though it's still the highest-frequency mode of the adsorption complex. Σ⁺, 2000–2130 cm⁻¹.

modes.label: ν(M-C)
modes.note: The whole C-O unit translates rigidly toward and away from the metal atom it's bonded to — the metal-carbon bond itself stretching, distinct from the much stiffer (and much higher-frequency) internal C-O stretch above. No band in this dataset separately resolves it; it's a real but very low-frequency mode. Σ⁺, 400–480 cm⁻¹.

modes.label: Frustrated rotation
modes.note: In the gas phase this would be a free molecular rotation; tethered to the surface, it becomes a genuine (if soft) restoring-force vibration instead — the whole C-O axis tilting away from perpendicular and back, doubly degenerate (Π) since it can tilt in any direction around the surface normal. Under the surface IR selection rule, only a dynamic dipole component perpendicular to a metal surface survives image-charge cancellation; this purely lateral motion's dipole change is canceled, so it's formally IR-inactive in reflection geometry despite being a real vibration. Π, 400–600 cm⁻¹.

modes.label: Frustrated translation
modes.note: What would be free lateral diffusion across the surface in the absence of a binding site becomes, once trapped in the adsorption potential well, the lowest-frequency vibration of the complex — the whole C-O unit sliding sideways and back, doubly degenerate (Π) for the same reason as the frustrated rotation above. Also IR-inactive in reflection geometry by the same surface selection rule (lateral dipole change, canceled by the image dipole). Π, 40–80 cm⁻¹.

modes.label: ν(CO)
modes.note: C and O move apart and together along the bond — now bridging two metal atoms instead of one, which lowers the local symmetry from the continuous C∞v of linear (μ₁) coordination to the finite C₂ᵥ point group. The extra metal neighbor enhances π-backdonation further, red-shifting ν(CO) well below the linear/on-top value. A₁, 1850–2000 cm⁻¹.

modes.label: νₛ(M-C)
modes.note: Both metal-carbon bonds of the bridge stretch together, in phase — C (with O rigidly along for the ride) moving directly away from the line joining its two metal neighbors. No band in this dataset separately resolves it; like the linear topology's own M-C stretch, this is a real but very low-frequency mode. A₁, 350–420 cm⁻¹.

modes.label: νₐₛ(M-C)
modes.note: The two metal-carbon bonds of the bridge engage in a shearing tug-of-war instead — C shifting sideways along the bridge axis, one M-C bond shortening as the other lengthens. Lateral, so canceled by the image dipole under the surface selection rule (same reasoning as the linear topology's frustrated modes) — formally IR-inactive in reflection geometry. No wavenumber is reported for this mode; B₁ here follows one axis convention, but the source leaves open whether B₁ or B₂ is the more conventional label for this particular shearing direction.

modes.label: ν(CO)
modes.note: C and O move apart and together along the bond, now coordinated to either three metal atoms (3-fold hollow, fcc/hcp sites on close-packed (111)-type facets, C₃ᵥ) or four (4-fold hollow, (100)-type facets, C₄ᵥ) — combined into one simplified topology here since both share the same A₁ C-O stretch character and this dataset doesn't otherwise distinguish them. The extra metal neighbors drive the strongest π-backdonation of any coordination geometry, red-shifting ν(CO) below both linear and bridged values — lower still for 4-fold (more backdonating neighbors) than 3-fold. A₁, 1700–1880 cm⁻¹ spanning both site types.

modes.label: νₛ(CO)
modes.note: Both C-O bonds stretch in phase, outward and inward together. The oscillating dipole this produces points straight along the C₂ axis (the bisector of the C-M-C angle), making this totally-symmetric mode both IR- and Raman-active. A₁, 2020–2200 cm⁻¹.

modes.label: νₛ(M-C)
modes.note: Both C-O units (each treated as one rigid ligand) translate together, in phase, toward and away from the shared metal center — the two M-C bonds stretching in unison rather than the internal C-O bonds. No band in this dataset separately resolves it; this sits well below the C-O stretches above. A₁, 350–550 cm⁻¹.

modes.label: δ(C-M-C)
modes.note: The two rigid C-O ligands swing toward and apart from each other, in-plane, opening and closing the C-M-C angle — a genuine rotation of each ligand about the fixed metal center, exactly preserving both M-C bond lengths. No band in this dataset separately resolves it. A₁, 250–400 cm⁻¹.

modes.label: ρ(CO)
modes.note: The two rigid C-O ligands swing the same way together, like a pair of windshield wipers — the C-M-C angle itself stays constant, only its orientation relative to the rest of the structure changes. Both M-C bond lengths are exactly preserved, same rotation mechanism as the scissoring mode above, just same-sign instead of opposite-sign. B₁, 400–600 cm⁻¹.

modes.label: νₐₛ(CO)
modes.note: One C-O bond stretches outward while the other compresses inward, out of phase. The resulting dipole change is perpendicular to the C₂ axis but still within the molecular plane, making this mode strongly IR-active. B₂, 1980–2150 cm⁻¹.

modes.label: νₐₛ(M-C)
modes.note: One rigid C-O ligand translates toward the metal center while the other translates away, out of phase — the two M-C bonds stretching in antiphase rather than together. No band in this dataset separately resolves it. B₂, 300–500 cm⁻¹.

modes.label: ν(CO)
modes.note: C and O move apart and together along the bond, exactly as in the linear (μ₁) topology — but here the molecule is flipped end-for-end, binding the metal/cation through its oxygen rather than its carbon. On a purely electrostatic cation site, this reversed orientation polarizes the bond the opposite way from C-bonding, red-shifting ν(CO) below the free-gas value instead of blue-shifting it, even though both orientations occupy the very same site simultaneously, in equilibrium with one another. Σ⁺, 2105–2125 cm⁻¹.

modes.label: ν(CH)
modes.note: The C-H bond stretches — the key HCOO* marker band, since no other common surface species shares this exact C-H environment. Can fall into Fermi resonance with the δ(OCH)+νₐₛ(OCO) combination band, splitting into a doublet. The free formate ion has its own conventional ν-numbering in the vibrational-spectroscopy literature (this mode is commonly cited as ν₁), though the exact assignment order varies by source more than CO₂'s does.

modes.label: νₐₛ(OCO)
modes.note: One C-O bond lengthens as the other shortens, in antiphase — often cited as ν₄ of the free formate ion. The position of this stretch is itself sensitive to binding geometry.

modes.label: νₛ(OCO)
modes.note: Both C-O bonds stretch in phase — often cited as ν₂ of the free formate ion. Paired with νₐₛ(OCO) above; the splitting between the two (Δν) is itself diagnostic of binding geometry.

modes.label: δ(OCH)
modes.note: The C-H bond rocks relative to the O-C-O frame, changing the O-C-H angle — often cited as ν₃ of the free formate ion. Often overlaps νₛ(OCO) and isn't always separately resolved in a spectrum.

modes.label: νₐₛ(OCO)
modes.note: One terminal (non-anchored) oxygen pulls in toward the carbon while the other pushes away — the two surface-bound complex's terminal C-O bonds stretching out of phase — and the carbon itself leans slightly toward the oxygen that's moving in toward it. The single anchor oxygen (Oₛ) stays put. This large, asymmetric dipole change makes it typically the highest-frequency, most intense band in the spectrum — the highest of all six A′/A″ modes, so it's ν₁ under the standard decreasing-frequency-within-species convention (see the Notation box). Physical picture and wavenumber from Solis et al.'s Fig. 5 (their own figure numbers these modes differently — see the Notation box for why this page doesn't follow that). ν(C-O), A′, 1450–1490 cm⁻¹.

modes.label: νₛ(OCO)
modes.note: Both terminal oxygens stretch outward and inward together, in phase, while the carbon itself dips slightly toward the anchor oxygen (Oₛ) — which otherwise stays put. Second-highest of the five A′ modes, hence ν₂. Physical picture and wavenumber from Solis et al.'s Fig. 5 (see νₐₛ(OCO)'s note for why this page's index doesn't match their own figure). ν(C-O)+ν(C-Oₛ), A′, 1350–1370 cm⁻¹.

modes.label: ν(C-O)
modes.note: The free ion's true totally-symmetric stretch, ν₁ of D₃h — IR-inactive there, but resolved and IR-active once surface binding breaks that symmetry; the one stretch with no sym/asym partner, since it singles out whichever one oxygen ISN'T equivalent to the other two. For monodentate coordination the odd one out is the one surface-anchored oxygen, so this is mainly the C-Oₛ single-bond stretch to it — but the coupled ν(C-Oₛ)+ν(C-O) character in the label shows up as the two terminal oxygens also leaning slightly toward the carbon as it moves. Third-highest of the five A′ modes, hence ν₃. Physical picture and wavenumber from Solis et al.'s Fig. 5 (see νₐₛ(OCO)'s note for why this page's index doesn't match their own figure). ν(C-Oₛ)+ν(C-O), A′, 1050–1070 cm⁻¹.

modes.label: γ(OCO)
modes.note: Both terminal oxygens push straight out of the molecular plane together while the central carbon buckles back the opposite way — the only out-of-plane mode of the six, which is why it alone carries the antisymmetric double-prime (A″); every other mode here stays flat in-plane (A′). The anchor oxygen (Oₛ), which the plane itself is defined relative to, doesn't move. As the lone non-totally-symmetric mode, it's numbered last (ν₆) under the standard convention, even though its own frequency falls in the middle of the other five — see the Notation box. Physical picture and wavenumber from Solis et al.'s Fig. 5 (their own figure numbers this mode ν₃ instead — see νₐₛ(OCO)'s note). π, A″, 850–860 cm⁻¹.

modes.label: δ(OCO)
modes.note: The two terminal oxygens open and close their shared angle relative to each other, like a pair of scissors, while the carbon dips slightly toward the anchor oxygen (Oₛ) at the same time — the anchor oxygen itself stays put either way. Fourth-highest of the five A′ modes, hence ν₄. Physical picture and wavenumber from Solis et al.'s Fig. 5 (see νₐₛ(OCO)'s note for why this page's index doesn't match their own figure). δ(OCOₛ), A′, 740–780 cm⁻¹.

modes.label: ρ(OCO)
modes.note: A seesaw about the fixed anchor oxygen (Oₛ): the carbon tilts one way while both terminal oxygens swing slightly the OPPOSITE way, rather than changing their own mutual angle the way scissoring above does. The lowest-frequency of the five A′ modes, hence ν₅ (last among A′, just ahead of the A″ wagging mode below). Physical picture and wavenumber from Solis et al.'s Fig. 5 (see νₐₛ(OCO)'s note for why this page's index doesn't match their own figure). δ(OₛCO), A′, 680–700 cm⁻¹.

modes.label: ν(C-O)
modes.note: The free ion's true totally-symmetric stretch, ν₁ of D₃h — IR-inactive there, but resolved and IR-active once surface binding breaks that symmetry; the one stretch with no sym/asym partner, since it singles out whichever one oxygen ISN'T equivalent to the other two. For bidentate coordination the odd one out is the free, non-coordinated oxygen, so this is that oxygen's own terminal C=Oₜ stretch, pushing and pulling along its own bond axis — with the carbon itself recoiling slightly the opposite way. A₁, 1600–1650 cm⁻¹, the highest-frequency bidentate mode, well clear of the ring-stretch pair below.

modes.label: νₐₛ(OCO)
modes.note: Two of the three C-O bonds stretch oppositely (one lengthens, one shortens) while the third stays put — one component of the doubly-degenerate asymmetric stretch, ν₃ of the free CO₃²⁻ ion (D₃h); surface binding splits that degenerate pair and lowers the overall symmetry to C₂ᵥ for bidentate coordination. The two surface-bound C-Oᵦ bonds engage in this out-of-phase tug-of-war — one stretches as the other compresses — with the free oxygen leaning slightly the opposite way. B₂, 1250–1320 cm⁻¹.

modes.label: νₛ(OCO)
modes.note: The two non-surface-bound C-O bonds stretch in phase — the other resolved component of the same doubly-degenerate ν₃ pair (paired with νₐₛ(OCO) above). Both surface-pinned oxygens expand and contract their C-Oᵦ bonds in absolute unison; the free oxygen drifts slightly the opposite way as a small counter-motion. A₁, 1000–1070 cm⁻¹, symmetric stretch of the two coordinated oxygens.

modes.label: γ(OCO)
modes.note: The central C buckles out of the O-C-O plane toward the viewer while the free oxygen recoils the opposite way, back into the page — the out-of-plane bend, ν₂ of the free ion, non-degenerate so it doesn't split into two distinct motions on binding (though its frequency still shifts a little by topology). Both surface-pinned oxygens, which anchor the plane itself, stay fixed. B₁, 830–850 cm⁻¹ — the one mode whose out-of-plane motion actually flips the coordinate signs across the molecular plane, unlike every A₁/B₂ mode here.

modes.label: δ(OCO)
modes.note: Ring flattening: the inner Oᵦ-C-Oᵦ bound angles open and pinch symmetrically like a pair of scissors, entirely in-plane — shown here as the carbon and the free oxygen drawing apart from each other symmetrically, since the two surface-pinned oxygens that define the ring can't themselves move. One component of the doubly-degenerate in-plane bend, ν₄ of the free ion. A₁, 750–800 cm⁻¹.

modes.label: ρ(OCO)
modes.note: The other resolved component of the same doubly-degenerate in-plane bend as δ(OCO) above — here the carbon and the free oxygen tilt left and right together, rhythmically, rather than swinging toward/apart from each other; the two surface-pinned oxygens, the fixed pivot this tilts relative to, don't move. B₂, below ~550 cm⁻¹ — the lowest-frequency mode of the six, often outside the practical DRIFTS detection window.

modes.label: νₛ(CH₃)
modes.note: All three C-H bonds stretch in phase while C and the surface-bound O stay put — the methyl group's totally symmetric stretch, by analogy with the free CH₃ group's non-degenerate ν₁. Its position shifts in tandem with νₐₛ(CH₃) below.

modes.label: νₐₛ(CH₃)
modes.note: One C-H bond lengthens as another shortens, in antiphase, while the third stays put — one component of the methyl group's doubly-degenerate asymmetric stretch.

modes.label: δₛ(CH₃)
modes.note: All three H's swing away from (or toward) the C-O axis together — the methyl "umbrella" deformation, by analogy with the free CH₃ group's non-degenerate ν₂.

modes.label: δₐₛ(CH₃)
modes.note: Two H's rock in antiphase relative to the C-O axis while the third stays put — one component of the methyl group's doubly-degenerate asymmetric deformation.

modes.label: ν(CO)
modes.note: The CH₃ group (C plus all three H's, moving together as a rigid unit) stretches away from the fixed, surface-bound O. Frequency is the diagnostic for binding geometry: monodentate (one M-O bond) sits above ~1100 cm⁻¹, bidentate (O bridging two M centers, or sitting at a bridging-O vacancy) below it — independent of the methyl group's own stretch/bend modes above, which barely shift between the two.
